notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Long white plates with a single blue strip on the left; Portugal's usually have a yellow strip on the right.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Hollow bollard with a yellow-orange reflector at the front and two white dots on the back, which can also be blank.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Upside-down triangle pole tops with a slightly upturned bar on top, as in France.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: High-voltage lines on pylons are very common, more so than in other Mediterranean countries.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road markers with colourful borders (orange, green, yellow by road size) and a road code on top.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Hunting signs: a white sign starting "coto" and ending "caza", or one split diagonally in black and white. Found nowhere else.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Rounded A-type guardrails with yellow reflectors.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian crossing signs have eight stripes, the most in Europe.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Red borders on road signs run right to the edge, with no thin white rim.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are black with white arrows or blue with white arrows; single-arrow ones are rare.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Rural roads sometimes have dashed outer lines, which are almost absent in Portugal and Italy.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Romance language with ñ (unique to it), de/del contractions, and calle for street. Portuguese uses ç, lh, nh and -ão.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: No-parking signs at garages read "Vado permanente" with a town hall name after "Ayuntamiento de".

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Very varied: Atlantic forest to semideserts, high plateaus and big mountain ranges; mostly dry Mediterranean climate.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Catalan has à, è, ò, ç, "i" for and, and carrer for street. Dominant on signs in Catalonia and the Balearics, mixed in Valencia.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Basque looks unlike any other language, with many Z and K, and kalea for street. Signs are bilingual in the Basque Country and northern Navarre.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Galician resembles Portuguese but has ñ and no ç; streets are rúa and many names start with A, O, As or Os.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Landlines start with 9, then regional digits; the first two digits give a precise region.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Regional road codes on markers show the province or community, like SG for Segovia. Asturias has many local codes.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The far north is green and lush, hilly with hedges and meadows, a bit like Ireland, France or the UK.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Light grey rock, many pines and stone-wall architecture mark the mountains on the French border.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Flat cereal fields, with some sunflowers, across the middle of Castilla y León.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Strip of semi-desert with sandy soil and shrubs along the Ebro basin, from Navarre across Aragón.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Open fields dotted with holm and cork oaks are very common in Extremadura.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Arid, sandy land with rugged bare hazy mountains in Murcia and southern Alicante.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Huge olive plantations over rolling hills as far as the eye can see around Córdoba and Jaén.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Eucalyptus plantations line the north coast, with the most in Galicia.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: A squarer orange-reflector bollard with a white rear reflector is almost exclusive to Lleida and Tarragona.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: The standard bollard with a green top is exclusive to Extremadura.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Blue and yellow snow poles are unique to Andalusia.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Small square chevrons with a red arrow on white are exclusive to Murcia.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Street signs with a very elaborately decorated frame belong to Bilbao only.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Nearly black slate roofs dominate the northwest, ending abruptly in the east.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Raised granaries called horreos are common in Galicia and Asturias; Asturian ones are larger and squarer.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Whole towns of white-painted houses are common in Andalusia, including hillside ones near Málaga.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Low rock walls, Aleppo pine hills and whitewashed houses mark the Balearic islands.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Volcanic black soil, extreme aridity or odd off-looking scenery that still matches the country suggests the Canary Islands.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: The squarer orange-reflector bollard is extremely common in Las Palmas province in the Canaries.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: North African style flat-roofed houses in warm colours mark the two enclaves bordering Morocco.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Black and white guardrails are unique to Ceuta within the country.
